sections.title: 听力 A · 1—4
sections.transcript:
W: Nina, how was the language exchange yesterday?
M: Better than I expected. I nearly joined the online group because it was cheaper, but its live meetings took place while I was at work. The library group meets on Wednesday evenings.
W: Did you spend the whole session studying grammar?
M: No. We worked in pairs and described an object without naming it. My partner had to guess what it was. I made mistakes, but the task forced me to keep speaking.
W: Was the group large?
M: Twelve people registered, although only eight came. That was useful because everyone had more speaking time. Next week we are bringing a photograph connected with a journey.
W: Will you continue?
M: Yes, but I will not buy the full ten-week course yet. The organiser lets newcomers attend twice before deciding. I want to see whether the Wednesday schedule remains manageable when work becomes busy.
W: That sounds sensible.
M: I used to choose courses by the number of lessons. Now I care more about whether I can participate regularly.

options: Ask her employer to change hours.
questions.explanation: 新人可试听两次，她已参加一次。

sections.title: 听力 A · 5—8
sections.transcript: Marcus had planned to buy a power drill after discovering a loose shelf in his kitchen. At the shop, however, he realised that the model recommended online cost more than the shelf itself. A neighbour told him about a tool library operating from an old fire station. Members pay a yearly fee and may borrow common tools for three days. Marcus visited on Saturday expecting a complicated registration process. Instead, a volunteer checked his address, showed him a safety video and helped him select a lighter drill. She also asked about the wall. When Marcus said it was plasterboard, she explained that ordinary screws might not hold the shelf and gave him the correct fittings. He returned the drill on Monday, cleaned but unused: after measuring again, he found a pipe behind the planned hole. The library volunteer suggested a safe alternative position. Marcus was briefly disappointed, yet pleased that he had avoided damaging the pipe. He now thinks the most valuable part of the library is not cheap access to equipment but advice before a tool is used.

The shop had no suitable screws.
His neighbour offered him one permanently.

options: A pipe was behind the wall.

questions.explanation: 重新测量后发现墙后有管道。

questions.prompt: What does Marcus value most about the library?
options: Guidance offered before borrowing and use.
questions.explanation: 结尾明确强调建议比低价借工具更有价值。

sections.title: 听力 A · 9—12
sections.transcript: Good afternoon, science club members. Because strong wind is forecast, Saturday's water-testing activity will not take place beside the lake. We will meet in the school laboratory at ten, one hour later than originally planned. Please use the east entrance; the main building will be locked. The samples were collected this morning and labelled with the locations where they came from, so we can still compare water from three parts of the lake. You do not need to bring gloves or glass containers. Both will be provided. However, bring a pencil because ink may run if the recording sheet gets wet. Parents who offered to drive students no longer need to stay for the whole session, but we would appreciate two adults returning at twelve thirty to help carry boxes to the storage room. The club photographer will come next month instead, when we repeat the outdoor part. Today's change is disappointing, but laboratory testing requires steady tables and accurate measurements. Trying to protect delicate equipment beside a windy lake would leave less time for the actual investigation.

questions.explanation: 手套和容器提供，只要求带铅笔。

questions.prompt: Who are asked to return at 12:30?
questions.explanation: 请求两位原本开车的成年人回来帮忙搬箱子。

sections.title: 听力 A · 13—16
sections.transcript:
W: Peter, the railway archive has received another box of photographs. Shall I start scanning them?
M: Please wait. Last month's images were scanned quickly, but twenty files are now called unknown station. We need to identify what we can before creating more files.
W: Most photographs have nothing written on the back.
M: True, but this box came with a notebook. The numbers beside several names may match marks on the envelopes. First, place each photograph beside its envelope and enter the envelope number in the catalogue.
W: Should I use the date I can see on the station clock?
M: No. The clock may have stopped. Record visible evidence in the notes, but leave the date field empty unless the notebook confirms it.
W: What about the damaged photograph?
M: Put it in the grey folder. Our conservator visits on Friday and will decide whether it can be safely flattened.
W: I see why cataloguing comes first.
M: Exactly. A beautiful scan is not useful if future researchers cannot discover where the original came from.

sections.title: 听力 A · 17—20
sections.transcript: I enrolled in a weekend history course at a famous college two towns away. The brochure promised expert teachers and access to a remarkable collection, so the long journey seemed worthwhile. On the first Saturday, the outward train arrived comfortably before class. The difficulty came later: the final discussion ended at six, but the last direct train left at five forty. I missed it and reached home nearly three hours later. The college offered recordings, yet the discussion was the part I most wanted. Before withdrawing, I spoke to the tutor. She told me the same course was being offered at my local learning centre in a blended form. The monthly object-handling workshop would be face to face, while shorter lectures could be watched online. I transferred the following week. The local centre's collection is smaller, but the tutor comments on my written work within five days. I once believed the most impressive institution must provide the best education. I now judge a course by whether its design allows me to attend, practise and receive useful feedback consistently.

options: The direct train left before discussion ended.
questions.explanation: 最后讨论结束晚于末班直达列车发车时间。

questions.prompt: Which part did the speaker most want to keep?
questions.explanation: 说话人明确说 discussion 是最想要的部分。

questions.explanation: 本地课程每月一次实物活动。

questions.prompt: What changed the speaker's idea of a good course?
options: The ability to participate and get feedback regularly.
questions.explanation: 结尾用参加、练习、反馈重新定义课程价值。

sections.title: 听力 B · 21—25
sections.transcript: The Repair Skills Programme opens for new members on 14 September. It began in 2022 when six neighbours started sharing tools and teaching simple household repairs. Meetings are held at the community college on Thursday evenings, from 6:30 to 8:00. Annual membership is twelve pounds; people under eighteen join free with an adult. Complete the blue form at reception and attach one photograph. During the first month, members may borrow two tools at a time. The usual limit later is four. Before borrowing electrical equipment, everyone watches a safety demonstration. The October workshop covers safe tool maintenance and is designed for beginners. Please arrive ten minutes early because the side entrance is locked once teaching starts. Questions about membership should go to coordinator Maya Chen, not the college office. A printed guide is available, but members are also expected to ask when they are uncertain. The programme succeeds because experienced users share practical knowledge, while beginners return equipment clean and report any damage promptly. Members sometimes bring their own small repair projects, but paint, gas appliances and damaged batteries are not accepted. A tool must be reserved online before collection.

sections.title: 阅读 A · 26—30
sections.text:
At the point when Leo started working on the homework centre, the stated objective involved provide silent study desks only. Initially, the proposal looked convincing and attracted early support. Evidence gathered during testing demonstrated that many pupils did not know how to divide large assignments. That finding did not destroy the purpose of the scheme. It showed that the coordinators had understood the goal more clearly than the daily experience of the participants expected to take part.

The most serious barrier was that volunteers answered the same urgent questions repeatedly. The coordinator chose not to defend the original design, Leo invited users to describe exactly when and why the barrier occurred. Their answers were more effective than a simple satisfaction score. One group prioritised convenience, another required clear instructions, and a third group asked for enough time to become familiar with the change.

The revised approach was to offer short planning appointments alongside quiet study. A second decision was to publish a weekly planning sheet. Over the next four weeks, participation increased and fewer participants asked staff for emergency help. Several inexpensive adjustments together created the better result.

Even so, the figures were not conclusive. The revised system did not suit everyone, and the coordinators kept another option available. Nor did they regard the first month's increase as final proof. Weather, calendars and publicity could influence the figures.

In the organiser’s view, the lasting lesson was simple: support should teach independence rather than create dependence. An idea may appear excellent in a meeting and still create unnecessary barriers in practice. Careful observation gives participants a chance to improve an idea without abandoning its purpose. Success then becomes easier to define: not as perfect agreement, but as a service that more participants can use with confidence. The experience also reminded those involved that small practical details can strongly influence whether a good idea works. Rather than making quick claims, the coordinators continued to collect comments and adjust the programme carefully. The centre now records whether pupils begin assignments earlier, a more meaningful sign of independence than the number of questions asked at a busy desk.

options: Many pupils did not know how to divide large assignments.

options: No one had used the service.
questions.explanation: 第四段指出季节和宣传也会影响数字。

questions.prompt: What conclusion did Leo draw about useful support?

All public projects should follow one fixed model.
New equipment always solves community problems.
questions.explanation: 全文用具体案例说明：理解实际需要并持续调整，才能让改变有效。

sections.title: 阅读 A · 31—35
sections.text:
When Sarah first became involved with the mobile library, the plan was to visit every village on the same weekday. The early suggestion seemed workable and attracted early support. Observation during the trial showed that market days changed when residents were already in town. The underlying aim still had value. It showed that the organisers had understood the goal more clearly than the daily experience of the people expected to take part.

The evidence had clear limits. The revised system did not suit everyone, and the organisers continued to offer an alternative. They also avoided treating the first month's increase as final proof. Seasonal habits and publicity could both affect the figures.

The team therefore decided to adjust stops according to local travel patterns. They also agreed to send reminder messages on the morning of each stop. During the following month, participation increased and fewer people asked staff for emergency help. A set of small revisions, rather than costly equipment, produced the improvement.

The most serious difficulty was that older users missed visits when buses were delayed. Rather than insisting on the draft, Sarah invited users to describe exactly when and why the difficulty occurred. Their answers were more useful than a simple satisfaction score. Some people valued convenience, others needed clear instructions, and several wanted enough time to become familiar with the change.

In the organiser’s view, the lasting lesson was simple: a regular service can still remain flexible. A project can sound excellent in a meeting and still create unnecessary barriers in practice. Careful observation gives people a chance to improve an idea without abandoning its purpose. It also makes success easier to define: not as perfect agreement, but as a service that more people can use with confidence. The experience also reminded those involved that small practical details can strongly influence whether a good idea works. Rather than making quick claims, the organisers continued to collect comments and adjust the project carefully. Drivers also keep a paper log when mobile signals fail, ensuring that later route decisions include villages where digital responses are least likely.

sections.title: 阅读 A · 36—40
sections.text:
At the point when Omar started working on the community translation programme, the stated objective involved translate all notices word for word. Initially, the proposal looked convincing and attracted early support. Evidence gathered during testing demonstrated that literal translations were accurate but difficult to follow. That finding did not destroy the purpose of the scheme. It showed that the coordinators had understood the goal more clearly than the daily experience of the participants expected to take part.

Even so, the figures were not conclusive. The revised system did not suit everyone, and the coordinators kept another option available. Nor did they regard the first month's increase as final proof. Weather, calendars and publicity could influence the figures.

The revised approach was to test shorter versions with intended readers. A second decision was to use familiar examples and a clear layout. Over the next four weeks, participation increased and fewer participants asked staff for emergency help. Several inexpensive adjustments together created the better result.

The most serious barrier was that important instructions were hidden in long sentences. The coordinator chose not to defend the original design, Omar invited users to describe exactly when and why the barrier occurred. Their answers were more effective than a simple satisfaction score. One group prioritised convenience, another required clear instructions, and a third group asked for enough time to become familiar with the change.

In the organiser’s view, the lasting lesson was simple: communication is successful only when the reader understands. An idea may appear excellent in a meeting and still create unnecessary barriers in practice. Careful observation gives participants a chance to improve an idea without abandoning its purpose. Success then becomes easier to define: not as perfect agreement, but as a service that more participants can use with confidence. The experience also reminded those involved that small practical details can strongly influence whether a good idea works. Rather than making quick claims, the coordinators continued to collect comments and adjust the programme carefully. A bilingual parent group checks the final notices aloud, since a sentence that looks simple on paper may still sound unnatural in conversation.

sections.title: 阅读 B · 41—45
sections.text:
Five students comment on a proposed shared study room.

Anna: My shop closes at six, after the public study areas shut. One evening session would let workers use the room without asking for all-night opening. A timetable should include people with ordinary jobs.

Ben: Later access requires paid supervisors who understand the equipment and emergency rules. Existing college staff are already busy. The organisers should show how extra shifts will be funded before advertising longer hours.

Clara: Our previous revision room looked empty for two weeks because the notice appeared only on a hidden webpage. Once tutors announced it, every desk was used. A fair trial needs visible publicity before low demand becomes an excuse to close.

David: The last bus to my village leaves at seven. A room open until nine helps residents nearby, but it remains inaccessible to me. Transport links and step-free entry should be considered with the timetable.

Eva: I share a noisy flat, so quiet concentration is the main benefit. Group tutorials are useful, but they must not occupy the whole room. Please protect individual desks where speaking is discouraged.

All five support learning, yet they judge access differently. Their comments show why a simple increase in opening hours cannot answer every practical question. The centre will publish a short review so users can see which suggestions were accepted and why. This makes later decisions easier to understand. The organisers propose a six-week experiment, with attendance recorded by time of day rather than as one total. A short questionnaire will ask why visitors came, whether they found a desk, and what prevented classmates from attending. They will also compare electricity and staffing costs with actual use. The study room currently has twenty desks, four computers and one group table. Food is excluded, though covered drinks are allowed. If the evening trial succeeds, exam periods may receive extra sessions. These details matter because an apparently popular room can still fail the people who need quiet, safe and affordable access most.

sections.title: 阅读 C · 46—55
sections.text:
A digital skills clinic requires [46] planning. Its room must be [47] for people carrying laptops, and [48] routines help volunteers protect personal data. Printed cards [49] the steps for common tasks. A trained helper is always [50] when a visitor becomes uncertain.

At first, there was little [51] between the clinic and neighbourhood groups. Volunteers began offering [52] demonstrations in familiar places. An appointment system helped [53] waiting, while friendly invitations [54] hesitant residents to [55].

The clinic never promises to repair every device. Instead, it teaches users how to recognise safe websites, create strong passwords and store important files. Visitors work on practice accounts before changing real settings. After each session, they receive a short record of what they completed and what to try next. Monthly feedback has led to larger print, clearer signs and a slower beginners' hour. The project shows that confidence grows through patient explanation. Expensive machines alone cannot replace trust, privacy and the chance to practise a task more than once. The clinic also lends large-print instructions for home practice. Follow-up visits are optional, and users decide which skill they want to attempt next. Volunteer notes are anonymous and deleted after each visit. Anyone facing a serious security problem is directed to a qualified service rather than encouraged to experiment. This boundary protects both learners and helpers.

sections.title: 写作 · 56

chart.title: the percentage of adults attending community learning activities

questions.prompt: Write an essay of about 120 words based on the chart. Describe and interpret the chart briefly, and give your comments.
questions.explanation: 先概括五年总体趋势并引用起止数据，再解释可能原因，最后给出个人评价和一至两项可行建议。

sections.model: The chart shows changes in the percentage of adults attending community learning activities over five years. Overall, the figure moved steadily from 24% in 2021 to 56% in 2025. The clearest change occurred in the middle of the period, suggesting that more people gradually accepted this choice. In my view, the trend is encouraging because it reflects greater attention to convenient and responsible daily habits. However, rising numbers alone do not guarantee a good experience. Organisers should maintain reliable facilities, publish simple guidance and collect feedback from different users. They should also keep an alternative for people who cannot use the service easily. With careful management, the positive trend can continue and bring lasting value to the wider community.
